L69: ##### 2026 October 06
L70: ### cite50†How Grobid uses Crossref metadata to enrich bibliographic information L71: Crossref members register around 37,000 records daily. All this metadata is openly shared with the global scholarly community through our free APIs. We receive over two billion calls to our API each month, signalling its use by hundreds of tools and services worldwide, supporting the discovery and assessment of scholarly metadata. As part of a new series in our blog, we will spotlight the diversity of tools and integrations that rely on Crossref metadata to serve the scholarly community.
L72: In this initial post, we chat to Luca Foppiano, the developer and maintainer of Grobid1, to learn about how Grobid uses Crossref metadata to improve the extraction and enrichment of bibliographic information from scholarly PDFs.

L112: ## REST API
L113: 
L114: Our publicly available REST API exposes the scholarly metadata that members and trusted sources deposit with Crossref. This bibliographic metadata and much more—you will find funding data, license information, post-publication updates, ORCID and ROR IDs, and abstracts. You can search, facet, filter, or sample metadata from dozens of thousands of members from all around the world, and the results are returned in JSON format.
L115: The metadata is deposited directly by our members, who publish the content represented by each metadata record. This is complemented by trusted sources, such as cite58†Retraction Watch . You will also find other identifiers, such as ORCID for individuals, RORs for funders and affiliations, and more. In some cases we add these identifiers where they are missing in the original deposit. There is an overview of the available content at cite59†Crossref stats .
L116: No sign-up is required to use the REST API, and almost none of the metadata is subject to copyright, and you may use it for any purpose. Some abstracts contained in the metadata may be subject to copyright by publishers or authors.
L117: ## Quick start
L118: 
L119: Use cite60†https://api.crossref.org/†api.crossref.org as your base URL. Add one of the available endpoints to query works, journals, members, funders, licences, prefixes, or types. Here are some examples to get you started:
L120: I would like to…  | Example request
L121: --- | ---
L122: Use the polite pool  | cite61†https://api.crossref.org/works?rows=0&mailto=AUTHORIZED_PROVIDER_INSTANCE†api.crossref.org L123: Retrieve metadata for a Crossref DOI  | cite62†https://api.crossref.org/works/doi/10.1128/mbio.01735-25†api.crossref.org L124: Retrieve records for 10 content items  | cite63†https://api.crossref.org/works?rows=10†api.crossref.org L125: Find works in the journal Psychoneuroendocrinology, ISSN 03064530  | cite64†https://api.crossref.org/journals/03064530/works†api.crossref.org L126: ## Endpoints
L127: 
L128: The Crossref REST API provides a number of endpoints for querying different types of records. Each endpoint has request parameters and cite65†filters to enable you to retrieve the metadata you are looking for. For further details about each endpoint, its parameters, and to try them out, see the Swagger documentation at cite60†https://api.crossref.org/†api.crossref.org L129: Endpoint  | Metadata returned
L130: --- | ---
L131: /works  | A list of content items registered with Crossref. This endpoint has a large number of parameters and cite65†filters available.
L132: /works/{doi}  | A single metadata record for a Crossref DOI.
L133: /works/{doi}/agency  | The registration agency for the specified DOI (e.g., Crossref or DataCite).
L134: /journals  | A list of journals whose content with registered content items.
L135: /journals/{issn}  | Details of the journal with the given ISSN.
L136: /journals/{issn}/works  | A list of works in the journal with the given ISSN.
L137: members  | A list of all organisations that have registered metadata with Crossref.
L138: /members/{id}  | Details about the Crossref member with the specified member ID.
L139: /members/{id}/works/  | A list of works associated with the specified member.
L140: /prefixes/{prefix}  | The name and Crossref member ID of the steward of the specified prefix.
L141: /prefixes/{prefix}/works  | A list of works associated with the specified prefix.
L142: /funders  | A list of funders in the Open Funder Registry.
L143: /funders/{id}  | Metadata for the member with the given ID.
L144: /funders/{id}/works  | A list of works associated with the specified funder ID.
L145: /types  | A list of all work types used in Crossref metadata.
L146: /types/{id}  | Information about the specified work type, e.g. `journal-article`, `monograph`, `grant`.
L147: /types/{id}/works  | A list of works with the specified work type.
L148: /licenses  | A list of licenses used by registered content items.
L149: ## Content negotiation
L150: 
L151: The REST API can return single metadata records in a variety of formats through a process known as content negotiation. See the cite66†content negotiation page for more details.
L152: ## Report an issue
L153: 
L154: Have you detected something that you would like to report? It could be incorrect, confusing, or partial metadata. Please report it on our cite4†community forum†community.crossref.org or check our cite67†backlog†crossref.atlassian.net of bugs and feature requests to see if it has already been reported.

L112: ## Access and authentication
L113: 
L114: Anyone can access the REST API, no signup or registration is required. We offer the following access options:
L115: 
L116: Option  | How to authenticate
L117: --- | ---
L118: Public  | No authentication or identification.
L119: Polite  | Include your email address in the `mailto` parameter or `agent` header.
L120: Metadata Plus  | Include your API key in the request header as `Crossref-Plus-API-Token: Bearer [API key]`
L121: The option you choose affects the rate limits. We recommend the polite option so that we can contact you if there is an issue.
L122: 
L123: cite58†Metadata Plus is our premium service that offers higher rate limits and priority support, and is designed for those who wish to integrate Crossref metadata into production services. If you subscribe to the service, you receive an API key. You can test your API key using cURL:
L124: 
L125: `curl -I -H "crossref-api-key: Bearer [API key]" "https://api.crossref.org/v1/works"`
L126: If successful, the HTTP status code will be 200 (it will be 401 if the token is not valid) and the response header will contain `x-api-pool: plus`.
L127: ## Request limits
L128: 
L129: In order to make the data accessible to all and keep the service stable, we operate limits that apply to individual users.
L130: 
L131: Rate limits: These are included in the results headers under `x-rate-limit-limit` and `x-rate-limit-interval` and depend on the pool accessed by your request. This gives the maximum number of requests you can make in a given time period.
L132: Concurrent request limits: These limits restrict the number of simultaneous requests that can be made and are given in the `x-concurrency-limit` response header. To avoid exceeding these limits, check that previous requests have completed before sending the next one.
L133: 
L134: The following limits apply:
L135: 
L136: Pool  | Rate limit  | Concurrency limit
L137: --- | --- | ---
L138: Public  | 5  | 1
L139: Polite  | 10  | 3
L140: Plus  | 150  | None
L141: If you exceed the rate limits, you will receive a 429 HTTP response. In this case, wait a short while and try your request again at a lower rate or with fewer simultaneous requests.
L142: Rate limits are usually applied and removed automatically. In the rare case that we apply a block manually, we will first make an effort to contact you to resolve the issue. For this reason we strongly recommend providing a `mailto` parameter in all requests. Blocked users will receive a 403 HTTP response and you can contact our support team to ask for a block to be removed.
L143: ## Best practice
L144: 
L145: By using our REST API, you are part of our community that supports open access to scholarly metadata. We ask that you are considerate of other users and don’t take actions that will make the API unstable, and hence unusable for others. You can do this by:
L146:   * Caching responses so you don’t make the same requests repeatedly. Be considerate about the frequency with which you refresh your cache.
L147:   * Use the `mailto` parameter and specify a `User-Agent` header that identifies you and your script.
L148:   * Handle HTTP response codes and monitor response times. Back off if the response times start to increase.
L149: 
L150: See cite59†more recommendations about how to get the most from the API.

L69: ##### 2026 October 06
L70: ### cite50†How Grobid uses Crossref metadata to enrich bibliographic information L71: Crossref members register around 37,000 records daily. All this metadata is openly shared with the global scholarly community through our free APIs. We receive over two billion calls to our API each month, signalling its use by hundreds of tools and services worldwide, supporting the discovery and assessment of scholarly metadata. As part of a new series in our blog, we will spotlight the diversity of tools and integrations that rely on Crossref metadata to serve the scholarly community.
L72: In this initial post, we chat to Luca Foppiano, the developer and maintainer of Grobid1, to learn about how Grobid uses Crossref metadata to improve the extraction and enrichment of bibliographic information from scholarly PDFs.

L87: ### cite53†July 2026 board meeting summary L88: We’re providing a summary of the board’s July 2026 meeting. The July board meeting is our only in-person meeting. The board gathers for two days of strategic thinking and long-range planning, as well as conducting annual board business. This year, we focused on allocating surplus funds we have on hand to invest in a three-year project to redesign the content system.
L89: In a related discussion, we decided to lower content registration fees starting in 2027 because we’ve had a demonstrated history of generating surpluses, exceeding what we need to run Crossref. We also discussed the board structure, as part of our regular review of stakeholder governance. And we conducted annual board business, such as approving the audited financial statements and reviewed our risk register and mitigation plans.
L90: The cite54†resolutions are available on the dedicated section of our website, which also lists the members of the Board and offers further information about our governance.

L98: ### cite56†Improving how funding connects to research outputs L99: Starting today, funder names deposited in Crossref metadata without an identifier will be matched to ROR IDs, to support an open and connected cite31†Research Nexus . Funding information is an increasingly important part of the scholarly record. The improved matching strategy supports researchers, funders, institutions, and meta-researchers, who rely on that information to understand how research is supported and what outcomes that support produces.

L112: ## Tips and tricks
L113: 
L114: We love to share our data and we want it to be used. Yes, really—and by as many people as possible. Here we share tips to help you get the most out of our REST API. Everyone benefits if you use our REST API responsibly and efficiently. Very occasionally we have had to block users who misuse our APIs, usually through carelessness rather than malice. If you follow the advice on this page you should have no problem.
L115: Note that for conciseness, the examples on this page omit the API URL, which is cite58†https://api.crossref.org/v1†api.crossref.org , so for an example like `/members/120` the full query is cite59†https://api.crossref.org/v1/members/120†api.crossref.org .

L127: 
L128: If you are just getting started with our API, we recommend heading to the cite68†API Learning Hub . There you can get to grips with APIs, what kind of metadata you can retrieve, and how to formulate queries. For a description of the endpoints and request parameters, see our cite69†Swagger documentation†api.crossref.org , where you can try out some queries.
L129: ### Get the right endpoint
L130: 
L131: Most of our queries go through the `/works` endpoint. If you’re looking for research outputs such as journal articles, that’s probably where you want to start.
L132: Bear in mind that we also have cite70†other endpoints , including `/prefixes`, `/journals`, and `/members`. You can, for example, get all works in a journal by using its ISSN, e.g.: `/journals/0003-3804/works`. The members endpoint contains summary metadata about organisations that have deposited metadata, including which metadata fields they deposit and the fraction of records with certain properties e.g.: `/members/120`.
L133: ### Use filter and query parameters
L134: 
L135: Our API contains a range of parameters that can be used to pull out records that match certain criteria. For example, various kinds of date filters: `/works?filter=from-pub-date:2024-01-01,until-pub-date:2025-12-31` will get all records with a publication date in 2024.
